The Lighthouse Keeper's Logbook

By Marta Quill

This is a dummy article written only to test url2epub from end to end. Every night for thirty-one years, the keeper of the Saltmarsh light wrote three lines in a leather logbook: the weather, the ships she saw, and one thing she had learned. The logbook survived two floods, a fire in the storeroom, and a curious goat, and today it sits in a glass case at the harbour museum, open at a page from the winter of 1974.

Reading it, you notice how little changes from night to night, and how much that small sameness matters. The wind turns, the tide comes in, a trawler passes at nine and another at half past ten. The keeper's handwriting tightens in storms and loosens in summer, and her lessons range from the practical, such as how to fix a cracked lens with resin, to the oddly profound, such as the note that fog is only a cloud that came down to listen.

Chapter one: The weather column

The first column is the weather, written in a shorthand the keeper invented herself. A circle with a dot means calm, a circle with a line means a breeze from the west, and a circle crossed twice means a gale that rattles the window frames. Meteorologists who studied the logbook found that her notes matched the official records closely, and in a few cases they caught squalls that the coastal station missed entirely.

Chapter two: The ships

The second column lists ships, by name when she could read it and by shape when she could not. Over three decades the list grows to more than eleven thousand entries, with the same fishing boats returning season after season, like old friends knocking at the door. Some names vanish abruptly, and a later line, written in smaller letters, sometimes explains why: sold, renamed, or lost with all hands in the March storms.

Chapter three: One thing learned

The third column is the reason people still visit the museum. One thing learned, every night, without exception. Some entries are jokes, some are recipes, and some are only a single word, but together they read like a slow conversation between a person and the sea. The last entry, dated the night before she retired, says simply: keep the light clean, and the ships will find their own way home.
